material:
Project: SparseRoute, a learned router for mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference.
- Problem: MoE layers send each token to the top-k of E experts. At inference, load imbalance leaves some GPUs idle while others queue. Measured on a 64-expert model: the busiest expert gets 3.1x the mean load (ours, Sec. 4).
- Closest work: Shazeer et al. introduced sparsely gated MoE [shazeer2017moe]. Switch Transformer simplified routing to top-1 [fedus2022switch]. GShard added a capacity limit and random dispatch [lepikhin2021gshard]. None of them adapts routing to the load seen at inference.
- Prior routers are known to be unstable during training (no citation in the library yet).
- Our contribution: (1) a router head trained with a load-balancing loss that is also applied at inference, (2) a drop-free dispatch scheme, (3) 1.4x higher throughput than GShard dispatch on 64 experts, at equal perplexity (Sec. 5).
- Venue: peer-reviewed ML conference, 1 page for the introduction.

Project: PatchGate, a token-dropping method for vision transformers.
- Problem: ViT cost grows quadratically with the number of patch tokens [dosovitskiy2021vit]. Many tokens in background regions add little.
- Our method scores each token with a 2-layer MLP and drops the lowest 40% before layer 4.
- Results: on ImageNet-1k with a ViT-B, top-1 accuracy 81.9 vs 82.3 for the full model, and 1.5x fewer FLOPs. We only ran ViT-B and ImageNet-1k.
- The author's notes say: 'we are the first to show token dropping works for vision transformers' (the author has not checked the literature for this).
- ResNets [he2016resnet] have no such token structure, which is why this is specific to transformers.
- Contributions: the scoring head, the drop schedule, the ImageNet-1k results.

request: Write the abstract from the finished text.
material:
Finished text of 'Rule Sets for Tabular Drift Detection'.
Introduction (summary): production models silently degrade when feature distributions drift. Statistical tests flag drift but give no account of which input region changed.
Method (summary): we fit a shallow decision tree on a drift label (reference vs current window) and read its leaves as axis-aligned rules that describe where the distributions differ. A stability filter keeps only rules that reappear in 8 of 10 bootstrap resamples.
Results (summary): on 12 public tabular datasets with injected drift, the rules recover the drifted region with mean F1 0.74; a two-sample test baseline gives no region. On one real credit-scoring log, the rules named the two features an analyst later confirmed as the cause.
Discussion (summary): the method assumes the drift is axis-aligned; rotated drift is described by many small rules. We did not test on text or images.
Conclusion (summary): rule-based drift reports are a practical complement to tests.

request: Write the results section for the main comparison.
material:
Main comparison (Table~\ref{tab:main}), mean F1 over 12 datasets, 5 seeds each:
| Method | F1 | Regions found |
| KS-test per feature | n/a | none |
| Isolation forest | 0.52 | partial |
| Ours (no stability filter) | 0.66 | yes |
| Ours | 0.74 | yes |
Notes: our best case is dataset 'adult' with F1 0.91, worst is 'covertype' with F1 0.48. The stability filter costs 9 seconds per run on average, versus under 1 second without it. Differences between 'Ours' and 'Ours (no stability filter)' were significant at p < 0.05 on 9 of 12 datasets.
